content: Polishing and buffing are surface finishing processes that involve smoothing a workpiece using abrasives and tools such as work wheels or leather strops. Polishing typically employs abrasives that are adhered to the work wheel, whereas buffing uses loose abrasives applied to the wheel. Polishing is a more aggressive process, while buffing is gentler, resulting in a smoother and brighter finish. Contrary to popular belief, most mirror-bright finishes are achieved through buffing rather than polishing. Polishing serves various purposes, including improving the aesthetic appeal of an object, preventing contamination of instruments, removing oxidation, creating reflective surfaces, and preventing corrosion in pipes. In metallography and metallurgy, polishing is used to produce a flat, defect-free surface for microscopic examination of a metal's microstructure. Silicon-based polishing pads or diamond solutions are often utilized in the polishing process. Polishing stainless steel can also enhance its sanitary properties. Oxidation or tarnish on metal objects can be removed using metal polish or tarnish removers, which are also considered polishing processes. To prevent further oxidation, polished metal surfaces may be coated with wax, oil, or lacquer, especially for copper alloys like brass and bronze. The term chem-mechanical describes the action of a corrosive slurry on silicon during polishing. In this process, multiple rotating heads, each fitted with silicon wafers, are pressed against a large rotating buffing pad immersed in a corrosive slurry. Material removal occurs at elevated temperatures through oxidation, followed by oxide removal via abrasion. This cycle repeats with each rotation of the head. A slurry can be created by combining potassium hydroxide and silox (a white paint base) with deionized water. The type of abrasive used in polishing depends on the condition of the metal. For unfinished materials, the process begins with a coarse abrasive (e.g., 60 or 80 grit) and progresses through finer abrasives (e.g., 120, 180, 220/240, 320, 400 grit, and higher) until the desired finish is achieved. Coarse abrasives remove surface imperfections such as pits, nicks, lines, and scratches, while finer abrasives leave progressively finer lines that are invisible to the naked eye. Achieving a 8 Finish (Mirror) requires polishing and buffing compounds, polishing wheels, and high-speed polishing machines or tools like electric drills. Lubricants such as wax and kerosene may be used for lubrication and cooling, although some polishing materials are designed for dry use. Buffing can be performed manually with stationary polishers or die grinders, or it can be automated using specialized equipment. Buffing involves two types of motions: the cut motion and the color motion. The cut motion produces a uniform, smooth, semi-bright surface finish by moving the workpiece against the rotation of the buffing wheel with medium to hard pressure. The color motion creates a clean, bright, shiny surface finish by moving the workpiece with the rotation of the buffing wheel using medium to light pressure. When polishing softer metals like brass, impurities often leave minute marks on the surface. To smooth these marks, the surface is polished with very fine (600 grit) abrasives, copper-plated, and then buffed to a mirror finish using an airflow mop. For a fine finish without plating, four operations are required: roughing, dry fining, greasing, and coloring. Roughing is typically performed on a solid grinding wheel, and for an extra fine polish, the greasing operation may be divided into rough greasing and fine greasing. However, for cost-saving purposes, inexpensive items may only undergo the first two operations. Polishing knives and cutlery, known as fine glazing or blue glazing, is technically a buffing operation because it uses loose abrasives but removes a significant amount of material, similar to polishing. Aluminum oxide abrasives are used for high-tensile-strength metals like carbon and alloy steel, tough iron, and nonferrous alloys. Silicon carbide abrasives are suitable for hard and brittle substances like gray iron and cemented carbide, as well as low-tensile-strength metals like brass, aluminum, and copper. Polishing wheels come in various types to meet different needs. Common materials for polishing wheels include wood, leather, canvas, cotton cloth, plastic, felt, paper, sheepskin, impregnated rubber, canvas composition, and wool, with leather and canvas being the most common. Wooden wheels with glued abrasives like emery are used for polishing flat surfaces and maintaining sharp edges. Cloth wheels vary in hardness; cemented cloth wheels are very hard and used for rough work, while sewn and glued cloth wheels are less aggressive. Some cloth wheels are not glued or cemented but are sewn and supported with metal side plates. Solid felt wheels are popular for fine finishes. Hard roughing wheels can be made by cementing strawboard paper disks, while softer paper wheels are made from felt paper. Most wheels operate at approximately 7500 surface feet per minute (SFM), but muslin, felt, and leather wheels typically run at 4000 SFM. Buffing wheels, also known as mops, are made from cotton or wool cloth and are available in bleached or unbleached forms. Specific types include sisal, spiral-sewn, loose cotton, canton flannel, domet flannel, denim, treated spiral-sewn, cushion, treated vented, untreated vented, string buff, finger buff, sisal rope, mushroom, facer, tampered, scrubbing mushroom, hourglass buff, rag, B, climax, swansdown, airflow, cool air, and bullet. A chart is often used to determine the appropriate wheels and compounds for polishing different materials, though experienced polishers may adjust materials to suit specific applications. Polishing is used to enhance and restore the appearance of metal parts or objects such as those on cars, handrails, cookware, kitchenware, and architectural metal. In industries like pharmaceuticals, dairy, and specialty plumbing, pipes are buffed to prevent corrosion and eliminate areas where bacteria or mold could reside. Buffing is also employed in the manufacturing of light reflectors.
